title: Proteins at work after a meal
body: After a meal rich in carbohydrates and proteins, many different proteins in the body go to work. In the small intestine, the enzyme trypsin breaks down dietary proteins into smaller peptides. As glucose from digested starch enters the blood, the pancreas releases the hormone insulin. Insulin signals muscle and fat cells, and a membrane protein called GLUT-4 then enables glucose to be transported into these cells. Meanwhile, antibodies in the blood continue to fight any infectious agents that entered with the food, and collagen, the most abundant protein of the animal world, forms part of the intercellular ground substance that holds tissues together. Receptor proteins on the tongue and in the nose allow the person to sense the taste and smell of the meal.

title: Temperature and an enzyme from liver
body: A student extracted an enzyme from goat liver and measured its activity at different temperatures, keeping the pH, the amount of enzyme and the substrate concentration the same in every tube. The relative activity (highest value taken as 100) was: 10 °C - 15; 20 °C - 35; 30 °C - 70; 37 °C - 100; 45 °C - 60; 60 °C - 5. The student then took two fresh samples of the same enzyme. Sample X was kept at 10 °C for one hour and Sample Y was kept at 60 °C for one hour. Both samples were then brought back to 37 °C and their activity was measured again.
